R Project Sprint 2026

R Project Sprint 2026 was a three-day event at the University of Birmingham, UK, that brought together novice and experienced contributors to work alongside members of the R Core Team. 36 members of the R community participated, with external contributors selected to balance technical expertise and provide opportunities for members of historically under-represented groups. Participants worked collaboratively on contributions to base R, CRAN maintenance, and infrastructure supporting contribution. Several small tasks were completed within the duration of the sprint and the event also provided an opportunity to discuss and prototype ideas for larger changes.

Heather Turner https://www.heatherturner.net/ (University of Birmingham) , Gabriel Becker (Independent consultant)
2026-10-20

1 Introduction

R Project Sprint 2026 was a three-day event hosted at the University of Birmingham, UK. The aim of the event was to bring novice and experienced contributors together to work collaboratively with members of the R Core Team, who maintain and develop the code and documentation that forms the base distribution of R (“base R”).

This was the second R Project Sprint, following the successful inaugural event in 2023 (Turner and Becker 2023). The sprint was organised as part of the Research Software Maintenance Fund (RSMF) project Enabling the Next Generation of Contributors to R, which incorporated plans for one sprint in Europe and a second sprint in the USA in 2027. Core funding for the sprint was provided by the R Consortium, covering the venue, catering and travel bursaries, while the R Foundation provided additional travel support for R Core developers.

2 Participants

Members of the R Core Team, RSMF project team, or the Bug Triage and Patch Team were guaranteed a place if they could partipate. This accounted for 18 participants including 7 members of the R Core Team. Another 18 participants - along with a couple more who were ultimately unable to participate - were selected from the self-nominated applicants. Figure 1 shows group photos taken on Day 1 and Day 3 of the sprint, a full list of participants is on the sprint website. Participation was in-person by default, but exceptions were made in a few cases where travel was not possible, e.g., due to visa issues or caring commitments.

Figure 1: Photos of sprint participants on Day 1 (top) and Day 3 (bottom) including online participants on screen (not all participants photographed).

Members of demographic groups underrepresented within the contributor community were encouraged to apply for a place, by promoting the event to affinity groups (R-Ladies+, rainbowR, and LatinR) and by direct communication with potential participants. Figure 2 shows the country of residence for the 36 participants. There were 18 based in Europe with 10 from the UK; 7 based in Latin America; 6 from the USA; 4 based in Oceania, and one based in India.

Figure 2: Choropleth showing the distribution of participants’ country of residence on the world map.

Compared to the sprint in 2023, there was lower representation of people based in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. We received only a small number of applications from these regions, possibly due to a shorter lead time, making it less feasible for people that would need a visa to attend in person. Although remote participation was an option, it was preferred to offer this to contributors with some experience, who could work more independently. Since 2023, we have been running R Dev Days, where it is easier to support new contributors in person or online.

Of the 25 participants that consented to share further demographic information, 16 may be regarded as underrepresented in the R developer community due to gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and/or disability status. There were 7 participants that identified as Arab, Asian or Pacific Islander, Black/African/Caribbean, or from Indigenous, aboriginal, or multiple ethnic groups.

The selection committee assessed the experience of the invited/selected contributors based on the information in their nomination form and/or personal knowledge. In contrast to 2023, a new category of “novice” was introduced - this was applied to people with a little experience of R contribution, typically from attending an R Dev Day. As can be seen in Figure 3, most participants had at least this level of experience, reflecting the impact of outreach initiatives in recent years. However, the selection committee still aimed to balance the numbers of novice/beginner contributors against the number of advanced contributors or core developers. For this sprint, we focused on programming contributions rather than translation contributions, which are better suited to the R Dev Days or short hackathons.

Figure 3: Histogram of participants’ level of expertise in R contribution, as judged by the selection committee.

3 Preparation

There were two sides to preparation for the sprint: gathering suitable tasks to work on and helping participants brush up their knowledge and skills.

Several tasks were proposed by R Core Team, others were selected issues from R’s Bugzilla (https://bugs.r-project.org), or proposed by the sprint participants. Following the practice of recent R Dev Days, proposed tasks for the sprint were gathered on a GitHub project board. This allowed issues to be added from existing GitHub repositories, such as the one used for R Dev Days or the one used by the translations infrastructure team, as well as allowing fresh ideas to be proposed. The board provided a way for participants to assign themselves to issues and record the progress of tasks.

In the lead-up to the sprint, new contributors were encouraged to watch YOU can contribute to base R!, a video recording of a recent Data Science Lab where Ella Kaye demonstrates working through a bug fix using the R Dev Container, and then to practice the basic contribution workflow themselves by working through the “Building R” and “R Contribution Workflow” tutorials in the R Dev container docs. Participants were also pointed of a list of further learning resources maintained on the R Dev Day repository.

4 Format

Each sprint day started with a kick-off session and ended with a report-back session, both hybrid to include our online participants. The remaining time was spent working in small groups, sometimes arranging hybrid meetings to discuss specific issues. A room laptop was kept connected to the online sessions set up for remote participants, so that it was easy for in-person participants to chat to remote participants on an ad-hoc basis.

In the kick-off session on the first day, Martin Maechler gave a 10 minute overview of how people can contribute to base R, highlighting some particular projects. All the R Core members present gave a brief introduction to themselves, highlighting their areas of interest and any particular issues they wanted to work on at the sprint. On the second day, Mikael Jagan gave a 10 minute talk on his experience as the newest member of the R Core Team. Beyond these introductions, participants used the daily kick-off sessions to collectively match people to tasks and raise any requests for help or make other announcements.

The report-back sessions were used to review progress and give an opportunity for quick questions or feedback. For the second report-back session, we were joined remotely by members of the University of Birmingham R User Group - several in-person participants were also members of this group, so it was nice to be able to share progress with them.

Both lunch and dinner were provided at the conference venue, except on the last day when those who were able to stay ventured out to some local places for dinner.

5 Contributions to R

The main focus of the sprint was the development of code and documentation in the base R distribution. Figure 4 shows the progress of related issues at the end of the sprint and two months after. An issue is considered closed if a corresponding bug report on R’s Bugzilla was closed or if a corresponding patch was committed to base R. By the end of the sprint, five issues had been closed, with patches for more than two-thirds of the remaining 22 issues.

Two months after the sprint…

Figure 4: Status of issues at the end of the sprint and two months after

Package-related issues included preventing leakage between package vignettes, adding support to load multiple packages in one library() call, developing an approach to inline images in HTML help, and various issues related to broadening the support for package binaries, e.g., enabling custom binaries on Windows.

The low-level issues included adding a warning when a logical subscript is fractionally recycled, developing a proposal for a hierarchy of typed errors, and adding support to register a function to be called before an expression is evaluated.

Issues related to general R development included detection of Fortran (and other) compilers in R’s configure, proposing a system to manage deprecation, and developing a script to install a set of minimal packages to run make check-all.

Statistics issues included developing an SE generic and methods, improve the error message for failed contrasts<- in model.matrix.default, and testing the updated algorithm for computing Kendall’s tau.

The main issue for translation was to prepare a patch of recent translations contributed via the community-maintained Weblate instance. Following discussions at R Dev Day @ useR! 2026, there was also work to change how the source location of translated strings is recorded in the translation files, reducing churn in version control. An investigation of potential solutions to retrieving the English error message after an error has been thrown in another language moved to a proposal after the sprint, which would become possible if the proposal for typed errors is implemented.

The miscellaneous issues were improving subsetting of rle objects and ensuring path.expand('~') returns UTF-8.

Finally there was one graphics issue, regarding white stripes on Cairo images.

6 CRAN packages and CRAN support

Although the R Project Sprint focuses on base R, some tasks were proposed to contribute to CRAN packages due to changes in the development version of R or changes in the CRAN checks. These included fixing unintentional use of fractional recycling in survival and patching packages relying on internal classes used in method dispatch. There was continued work on fixing the “Lost braces” NOTE on CRAN packages, which not only resulted in patches to nearly 20 packages, but also implemented automated tracking using an online spreadsheet, for use by contributors and CRAN maintainers.

Another task related more directly to supporting the CRAN Team: developing code to create issues on GitLab or Codeberg to ask for a new maintainer email.

7 Translation and translation infrastructure

The sprint provided an opportunity for Gergely Daróczi, who set up the Weblate instance in 2022, to onboard Bea Fernandez and Fernando Corrêa as administrators. In addition to collaborating on the translation patch, they made a fresh checkout of the .po files from the R SVN repository and updated the Weblate configuration to reduce the ad-hoc fixes required to generate a clean patch.

The team also worked to unlock Weblate components for the recommended packages that had been locked due to git conflicts. They identified an improved configuration that would avoid one type of issue in future.

Although it was not a main task at the sprint, one participant did join the Weblate instance and added a few French translations in between other tasks!

Another translation-related activity was testing the rdlocal package, updated by Aditya Bansal in a Google Summer of Code project to provide prototype infrastructure for adding multilingual help pages to an R package. This was the latest development in work that came out of a discussion at R Project Sprint 2023, carried forward by Elio Campitelli, who mentored the GSoC project and joined the 2026 sprint remotely from Australia! Testing at the sprint revealed a number of issues and pull requests were made to fix several of them. Interested contributors are welcome to work on the remaining open issues.

8 Contributor infrastructure

A number of participants worked on an accessibility audit of the R Contributor Website, the R Development Guide and the R Dev Container Docs. The team opened issues on the relevant repositories where improvements were needed and opened pull requests to fix several of these issues.

Other work on contributor infrastructure included testing and revising the instructions for installing R from source on macOS, for later addition to the R Dev Guides

9 Summary

R Project Sprint 2026 was a productive event, where participants made a wide variety of contributions to base R, CRAN packages and infrastructure supporting contribution. Although the R Dev Days have provided a way to engage the broader community in contribution on a more regular basis, the longer sprint format allows more time for discussion, tackling bigger issues and learning from each other.

We look forward to the next sprint, planned for week beginning April 12, 2027, in Boston, USA.
